# T200 Rod-Lift Oil Well — Operating & Maintenance Manual

> Fictional manual written for the FlytBase Asset Copilot hackathon. Modelled on typical
> sucker-rod (beam pump) well practice. Not for real-world operational use.

Document ID: OM-T200 · Revision 4 · Applies to all wells with `well_type = "T200"`

## 1. Scope

This manual covers the T200 class of onshore rod-lift (beam pump) oil wells: a
conventional wellhead, a surface pump jack (walking-beam pumping unit), a sucker
rod string, an insert downhole pump and a 3-inch carbon-steel flowline to the
area gathering line. Some T200 pads also carry a two-phase vertical separator.

## 2. Equipment overview

| Equipment | Typical model | Function |
|---|---|---|
| Wellhead | WH-3000 | Seals the well, holds the stuffing box and production valves |
| Pump jack | PJ-228 | Converts motor rotation to reciprocating rod motion |
| Rod string | API Grade D 7/8 in | Transmits motion from the pump jack to the downhole pump |
| Downhole pump | Insert rod pump 1.75 in | Lifts fluid from the reservoir |
| Flowline | 3 in carbon steel | Carries produced fluid to the gathering line |
| Separator (optional) | 2-phase vertical 24 in | Separates gas from liquid on the pad |

## 3. Normal operation

A producing T200 well cycles continuously at 6–9 strokes per minute. Produced
fluid leaves the reservoir warmer than the surface air, so a producing wellhead
runs noticeably warmer than ambient. When the pump stops, the
wellhead cools to near ambient within a few hours.

Operators should expect daily and seasonal variation. On hot summer afternoons
the steel of an idle wellhead can read well above 45 °C from solar heating alone.
**Never judge production from absolute wellhead temperature.**

## 4. Start-up and shut-in

1. Confirm the flowline valve is open and the separator (if fitted) is at operating level.
2. Release the pump jack brake and start the prime mover.
3. Confirm stroke rate within 6–9 spm and check the stuffing box for leaks.
4. For a planned shut-in, stop the prime mover at the bottom of the stroke, set the brake,
   close the wing valve and record the shut-in in the maintenance system before work starts.

## 5. Routine inspection checklist

- Visual check of pad, cellar and flowline route for staining or pooled fluid.
- Thermal reading of the wellhead (drone or handheld).
- Stuffing box leakage, belt condition and gearbox oil level.
- Separator level and dump valve operation (if fitted).

## 6. Lubrication schedule

| Item | Interval |
|---|---|
| Saddle and tail bearings | 90 days |
| Gearbox oil level check | 30 days |
| Gearbox oil change | 12 months |
| Belt tension | 60 days |

## 7. Common failure modes

| Symptom | Likely cause | First action |
|---|---|---|
| Unit running, wellhead cold | Rod parted or pump stuck | Shut in, call rod/pump crew |
| Unit stopped, motor hot | Prime mover overload | Reset overload, check cooling |
| Oil on gearbox base | Seal failure | Replace seals |
| Staining along flowline | Corrosion pinhole or coupling failure | Shut in, contain, report per SOP SR |
| Stuffing box weeping | Worn packing | Replace packing |

## 8. Spill response on the pad

Any crude release must be handled under the company Spill Response SOP
(`sops/spill-response-sop.md`). In short: stop the source, contain, estimate the
volume, and report within the deadline set by the SOP.

## 9. Engineering limits

### 9.1 Pressure
Maximum allowable wellhead working pressure: 3,000 psi.

### 9.2 Stroke
Maximum stroke rate: 10 spm. Maximum polished-rod load: 22,800 lb.

### 9.3 Production temperature rule
A T200 well is considered **producing (active)** when its wellhead temperature is
at least **15 °C above ambient** air temperature at the time of the reading. A
difference below 15 °C means the well is **not producing** for that reading,
whatever the absolute temperature.

### 9.4 Temperature alarm
The wellhead must stay **at or below 85 °C**. Any reading above 85 °C requires the
operator to shut in and inspect the stuffing box and rod string within 24 hours.

### 9.5 Spill-related shut-in
If a spill covers **more than 5 % of the pad area**, shut in the well immediately and
keep it shut in until the source is repaired.

## 10. Maintenance escalation

- Three or more **corrective** maintenance events on the same equipment kind in the
  12 months before the current date require a root-cause analysis (RCA) before the next repair is closed.
- Downtime of more than 14 consecutive days must be reported to the area production supervisor.
- An annual flowline integrity test is mandatory (see Regulatory Compliance SOP, RC-02).

## 11. Records

Every inspection, maintenance job and shut-in must be recorded. Human notes that
explain an abnormal reading (for example a planned shut-in) are valid context and
should be considered alongside the sensor data.

# T350 Deep Rod-Lift Oil Well — Operating & Maintenance Manual

> Fictional manual written for the FlytBase Asset Copilot hackathon. Not for real-world use.

Document ID: OM-T350 · Revision 2 · Applies to all wells with `well_type = "T350"`

## 1. Scope

The T350 is a deeper, higher-rate version of the T200 rod-lift well. It uses a
WH-5000 wellhead, a PJ-456 pump jack and the same rod, pump and
flowline families as the T200. Procedures not listed here follow the T200 manual.

## 2. Differences from T200

| Item | T200 | T350 |
|---|---|---|
| Wellhead rating | 3,000 psi | 5,000 psi |
| Pump jack | PJ-228 | PJ-456 |
| Normal stroke rate | 6–9 spm | 5–8 spm |
| Max polished-rod load | 22,800 lb | 45,600 lb |

## 3. Production temperature rule

Because T350 fluid comes from a deeper, hotter zone, a T350 well is considered
**producing (active)** only when its wellhead temperature is at least **20 °C above
ambient** air temperature at the time of the reading.

## 4. Temperature alarm

The wellhead must stay **at or below 95 °C**. Above 95 °C, shut in and inspect within 24 hours.

## 5. Spill-related shut-in

Same as T200: a spill covering more than 5 % of the pad area requires immediate shut-in.

## 6. Maintenance escalation

Same as T200 section 10 (RCA after three corrective events on the same equipment
kind within 12 months; report downtime over 14 consecutive days).
manuals_and_sops_verbatim.spill-response-sop.md:
# Spill Response SOP

> Fictional SOP for the FlytBase Asset Copilot hackathon. Simplified and modelled on
> common US onshore practice. It is not a copy of any rule and is not legal or regulatory
> guidance.

Document ID: SOP-SR · Revision 5 · Effective 1 Jan 2027 · Owner: Health, Safety & Environment (TEAM-HSE)

## Revision history

| Revision | In force for spills discovered | Change |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | from 1 Jan 2027 | SR-01 written notice deadline cut from 24 hours to **12 hours** |
| 4 | before 1 Jan 2027 | SR-01 written notice within 24 hours |

Use the revision that was in force on the date the spill was **discovered**.

## 1. Purpose

Defines how field teams respond to, classify, report and close out crude oil
releases on well pads and along flowlines.

## 2. Background (industry references)

- **Reporting:** state oil and gas regulators commonly require immediate notice of fires,
  leaks, spills and breaks, and a written report for crude oil losses of more than 5
  barrels. Texas Railroad Commission Statewide Rule 20 and its Form H-8 are an example. Our SR-01 keeps the
  immediate phone call and adds a company deadline for the written notice (12 hours from
  revision 5; 24 hours before).
  Our reporting threshold (5 bbl or more) is slightly stricter than "more than 5 bbl".
- **Cleanup:** Texas Statewide Rule 91 is an example cleanup standard for crude oil on
  land in non-sensitive areas. It requires free oil to be removed promptly, the
  contamination to be mapped, and soil cleaned to **1.0% total petroleum hydrocarbons
  (TPH) by weight**; Commission guidance also describes treating more heavily
  contaminated soil (around 5% TPH) by mixing it down or hauling it away. Our SR-03 follows
  this approach. The number of soil samples and the 60-day verification deadline in SR-03
  are company rules.
- **Prevention:** for onshore production facilities covered by EPA's SPCC rules,
  40 CFR 112.9 requires a flowline maintenance program and prompt cleanup of discharges
  (see Regulatory Compliance SOP, RC-05).

## 3. Spill classes

The classes, the 72-hour HSE notice and the 4-hour containment limit (SR-02) are company
rules.

| Class | Estimated crude volume | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Minor | below 1 bbl | Record and clean up; no external report |
| Moderate | 1 bbl to below 5 bbl | Record, clean up, notify HSE within 72 h |
| Reportable | 5 bbl to below 25 bbl | External report required (SR-01) |
| Major | 25 bbl or more | External report within 2 h (company rule), incident command |

1 bbl (barrel) = 159 litres.

## 4. Protocols

| Protocol ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **SR-01** | For a **reportable or major** spill, phone the State Oil & Gas Commission immediately, then file the **written notice** (volume, affected area, cleanup plan) within **12 hours** of discovery (24 hours for spills discovered before 1 Jan 2027), or within **2 hours** for a major spill. Discovery time is the time of the inspection that detected the spill. `hours_to_report` in the data is the time to the written notice. |
| **SR-02** | The source must be stopped and the spill contained within **4 hours** of discovery. |
| **SR-03** | Contaminated soil must be cleaned to **1.0% TPH or less**. Take **at least 4 soil samples** to map the edges of a reportable spill. Haul soil above 5% TPH to an approved disposal site. For reportable and major spills, the remediation must be **verified within 60 days** of discovery; verification is closed only by a passing site inspection from the environmental agency. Smaller spills are cleaned to the same 1.0% TPH target without agency verification. |
| **SR-04** | Every spill, including minor ones, must be recorded against the asset with an estimated volume and affected area. |

## 5. Response steps

1. Stop the source (shut in the well if needed; see the well-type manual).
2. Contain the spill (berms, absorbents).
3. Estimate volume and affected pad area.
4. Classify using section 3.
5. Report per SR-01 if required.
6. Repair the cause and log a corrective maintenance record.
7. Remediate, sample the soil and request agency verification (SR-03).
8. Write the maintenance report with a compliance check (Field Work SOP, WS-07).

## 6. Penalties

A late SR-01 report usually results in a **notice of violation** from the State Oil &
Gas Commission, typically with a fine between USD 2,500 and 7,500. An open notice
stays on the asset's compliance record until the agency closes it.

## 7. False positives

If a detected "spill" is later confirmed as water, mud or shadow by a qualified
person, that correction is recorded as a context note. Corrected detections do not
count as spills for reporting or statistics.
manuals_and_sops_verbatim.regulatory-compliance-sop.md:
# Regulatory Compliance SOP

> Fictional SOP for the FlytBase Asset Copilot hackathon. Not legal or regulatory guidance.

Document ID: SOP-RC · Revision 2 · Owner: Health, Safety & Environment (TEAM-HSE)

## 1. Purpose

Lists recurring compliance duties for every oil well asset and how they are evidenced in the records.

## 2. Protocols

| Protocol ID | Requirement | Evidence in the data |
|---|---|---|
| **RC-01** | Every well must be inspected at least once every **14 days**. | `inspections.jsonl` timestamps |
| **RC-02** | Every flowline must pass an **integrity test once per calendar year**. | `maintenance.jsonl` entries with issue "Annual flowline integrity test" |
| **RC-03** | Any well down for more than **14 consecutive days** must be reported to the area production supervisor. | Inspections plus context notes |
| **RC-04** | Agency notices of violation must be answered within **30 days** and tracked until closed. | `regulatory-events.jsonl` status and `nov_response_filed` events |
| **RC-05** | Keep a **flowline maintenance program**: weekly visual inspection of the pad and flowline route, corrective repair of any leak found, and prompt cleanup. Modelled on EPA SPCC rules for onshore production (40 CFR 112.9(d)(4)). | Inspections, flowline repairs and their reports |

## 3. External agencies

| Agency | Typical events |
|---|---|
| State Oil & Gas Commission | Spill reports, notices of violation, fines |
| Regional Environmental Protection Office | Site inspections, remediation verification |

## 4. Status values

Regulatory events are `open` until the agency confirms closure, then `closed`.
manuals_and_sops_verbatim.field-work-sop.md:
# Field Work Safety and Maintenance SOP

> Fictional SOP for the FlytBase Asset Copilot hackathon. Simplified and modelled on common
> US onshore practice and the public scope of industry documents named below. It is not a
> copy of any standard and is not real safety, legal or regulatory guidance.

Document ID: SOP-WS · Revision 2 · Owner: Field Maintenance (TEAM-MX) with HSE (TEAM-HSE)

## 1. Purpose

Defines how maintenance crews prepare for, carry out, test and close out work on a well:
the pump jack, rod string, downhole pump, wellhead, flowline and separator. Every
maintenance report must include a compliance check against the protocols below.

## 2. Background (industry references)

| Topic | What industry practice says | How this SOP uses it |
|---|---|---|
| Crew safety on well servicing | API RP 54 (*Occupational Safety and Health for Oil and Gas Well Drilling and Servicing Operations*) covers well servicing rigs and special services. Pre-job safety meetings (job safety analysis briefings) are standard practice in OSHA's oil and gas safety guidance. | WS-01 |
| Energy isolation | The federal lockout/tagout standard (OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147) lists oil and gas well drilling and servicing as outside its scope; the US Chemical Safety Board has recommended closing that gap. API RP 11G (*Installation, Maintenance and Lubrication of Pumping Units*) covers safe installation and servicing of beam pumping units, and the manufacturer's instructions take precedence. | WS-02 is our company rule |
| Hydrogen sulfide | API RP 49 covers drilling and well servicing where hydrogen sulfide (H2S) may be present; 10 ppm is the commonly used action level. | WS-03 |
| Hot work | API RP 2009 covers safe welding, cutting and hot work in the petroleum industry, including permits and gas testing. | WS-04 (the 10% LEL limit is our company rule) |
| Pressure testing | US rules for hazardous liquid pipelines (49 CFR 195.304) test at 1.25 × the maximum operating pressure (MOP) for at least 4 hours. ASME B31.4 bases its test on the internal design pressure. Flowlines on a lease are not always covered by these rules. | WS-05 is our company rule, modelled on 49 CFR 195.304 |
| Flowline maintenance | EPA SPCC rules for onshore production (40 CFR 112.9(d)(4)) require a flowline maintenance program: compatible materials, scheduled inspection or testing, corrective action, and prompt cleanup of discharges. | WS-05, WS-06 and RC-05 |

## 3. Protocols

| Protocol ID | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **WS-01** | Hold and record a **pre-job safety meeting** (job safety analysis) with the whole crew before any work starts. |
| **WS-02** | **Isolate energy** before touching moving or pressurised equipment. Stop the prime mover at the bottom of the stroke, set and chain the brake, lock and tag the motor disconnect, close and tag the wellhead wing valve, and bleed trapped pressure. Remove locks only after the crew lead confirms everyone is clear. |
| **WS-03** | Every crew member wears a **personal H2S monitor**, bump-tested that day. If any monitor reads **10 ppm or more**, stop work, move upwind, and do not return until readings are below 10 ppm and the HSE officer approves. |
| **WS-04** | Welding, cutting or grinding needs a **hot work permit** and a **gas test** first. No hot work while flammable gas reads **10% of the lower explosive limit (LEL) or more**. |
| **WS-05** | After any flowline repair, **pressure-test** the repaired section at **at least 1.25 × the flowline's maximum operating pressure (MOP)** and **hold for 4 hours** with no unexplained pressure drop before returning the well to production. |
| **WS-06** | Contaminated soil, absorbents and replaced parts with oil on them are **waste**. Bag or contain them on site, record the quantity, and ship them with a **waste manifest** to an approved disposal site. |
| **WS-07** | Write the **maintenance report** within 3 days of finishing the work. Include what happened, root cause, work done, parts, safety steps, tests, waste and a compliance check against this SOP and the Spill Response SOP. |

## 4. Typical work by equipment

| Equipment | Usual problems | Usual work |
|---|---|---|
| Pump jack | Bearing wear, gearbox oil leaks, prime mover (electric motor) trips or failure, belt wear | Replace bearings or seals, change gearbox oil, rewind or replace motor, re-tension belts, check counterbalance |
| Rod string | Parted (broken) sucker rod | Workover rig pulls rods, fishing tool recovers the broken part, damaged rods replaced |
| Downhole pump | Stuck or worn pump | Workover rig pulls rods and pump, pump replaced, well tested |
| Wellhead | Stuffing box packing leak, valve wear | Replace packing, service or replace valves, pressure test |
| Flowline | Corrosion pinhole leaks, coupling failures | Clamp or replace the section, pressure test (WS-05), clean up any release (SR-03) |
| Separator | Level controller faults | Replace or recalibrate controller, test dump valve |

## 5. Close-out

The crew lead confirms the well is producing again (or records why not), removes locks and
tags, and files the report (WS-07). HSE reviews every report with a "not met" item.

WELL-0001_june_2026.content:
# Maintenance Report — MNT-0001-029

**Asset:** WELL-0001 (SW-23 Well 001, T200, Southwest Block 23)
**Equipment:** flowline
**Work started:** 12 Jun 2026 07:00 · **Finished:** 13 Jun 2026 18:00 · **Well stopped for this job:** 35 hours
**Crew lead:** Daniel Foster (U-302) · **Crew:** Brian Coleman, Megan Ward · **Contractor:** Tumbleweed Flowline Co.
**Triggered by:** inspection INS-0001-0185 on 2026-06-11
**Report written:** 15 Jun 2026

## What happened

The weekly drone inspection INS-0001-0185 at 14:30 on 11 June 2026 found crude oil pooled
around the flowline coupling about 6 m downstream of the wellhead. Roughly 9.4% of the pad
was stained, an estimated 6.8 bbl. That is a reportable spill under the Spill Response SOP,
and because it covered more than 5% of the pad the T200 manual requires an immediate
shut-in. The field operator, Jake Morales, shut the well in that afternoon. The crew on
call was finishing another job, so earth berms and absorbent pads were only in place in the
evening: the release was **contained about 7 hours after the inspection flight**.

The spill report to the State Oil & Gas Commission was filed 41 hours after detection, on
13 June. The HSE on-call handover had been missed, so nobody owned the report on 11–12 June.

## Root cause

The threaded coupling had external corrosion under a failed protective wrap. This is the
second flowline failure in a month on this well: a pinhole leak was repaired on 10 May 2026
(MNT-0001-028). The flowline passed its annual integrity test on 7 March 2026
(MNT-0001-026). A pressure test does not reveal wall loss hidden under a wrap, so the
weakness was missed.

## Safety and permits

- Pre-job safety meeting held with the crew and the contractor before work started (WS-01).
- Energy isolated: prime mover stopped at the bottom of the stroke, brake set and chained, motor disconnect locked and tagged, wellhead wing valve and flowline valve closed and tagged, line pressure bled off (WS-02).
- Personal H2S monitors worn; highest reading 2 ppm, below the 10 ppm stop-work level (WS-03).
- Hot work permit issued for welding; gas test before welding read 0% LEL (WS-04).

## Work done

1. Removed free oil from the pad with a vacuum truck and absorbent pads.
2. Excavated around the coupling and exposed 6 m of flowline.
3. Cut out the failed coupling and 4 m of corroded pipe.
4. Welded in new pipe and a new coupling, then wrapped the joint.
5. Excavated the stained soil around the coupling and across the pad.

Summary of the fix: replaced coupling and 4 m of flowline; excavated and bagged contaminated soil.

## Testing and return to service

Pressure-tested the repaired section at 196 psi (1.25 × the flowline's maximum operating
pressure of 157 psi) and held for 4 hours with no pressure drop (WS-05). The well was returned to
production at 18:00 on 13 June.

## Spill clean-up and waste

- About 3.3 m³ of stained soil excavated, bagged and shipped to an approved disposal site under waste manifest WM-0001-029 (WS-06).
- 4 soil samples taken around the spill; the highest result after clean-up was 0.8% TPH, below the 1.0% target. Agency verification requested (SR-03).

## Parts and cost

| Item | USD |
|---|---|
| Line pipe, coupling and wrap | 2,350 |
| Absorbents, berms and vacuum truck | 1,100 |
| Soil hauling and disposal | 1,700 |
| Labour (about 64 crew-hours, contractor and company) | 7,400 |
| **Total** | **12,550** |

## Compliance check

| Protocol | Result | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| WS-01 | Met | Meeting held and recorded |
| WS-02 | Met | Energy isolated and tagged |
| WS-03 | Met | Monitors bump-tested; max 2 ppm |
| WS-04 | Met | Permit issued; gas test 0% LEL |
| WS-05 | Met | Tested at 1.25 × maximum operating pressure, held 4 hours |
| WS-06 | Met | Oily waste manifested to an approved site |
| WS-07 | Met | Written 2 days after the work |
| SR-01 | **Not met** | Reported to the State Oil & Gas Commission 41 hours after discovery (limit 24 hours) |
| SR-02 | **Not met** | Contained about 7 hours after discovery (limit 4 hours) |
| SR-03 | In progress | Cleaned to below 1.0% TPH; agency verification requested, due within 60 days |
| SR-04 | Met | Spill recorded with volume and area (reportable class) |

## Notes and recommendations

- HSE to fix the on-call handover so reportable spills always have an owner.
- Replace the whole flowline on this well instead of patching sections; two failures in a month show the line is in poor condition.
- Add a visual check of coupling wraps to the flowline inspection, because pressure tests miss wall loss under a wrap.

Summary of the fix: replaced the flange gasket and bolts and remediated soil.

## Testing and return to service

Pressure-tested the repaired section at 326 psi (1.25 × the flowline's maximum operating pressure of 261 psi) and held it for 4 hours with no pressure drop (WS-05). The well was returned to production.

## Spill clean-up and waste

- About 3.7 m³ of stained soil excavated, bagged and sent to an approved disposal site under waste manifest WM-0151-025 (WS-06).
- 2 soil samples taken around the spill; the highest result after clean-up was 0.26% TPH, below the 1.0% target (SR-03).
- Soil samples sent to the lab.
